quiz.q: In `std::env::args()`, what is the first element (`args[0]`)?
options: The first flag the user passed
quiz.explain: args[0] is the program name. The first real user argument is args[1].

quiz.q: Why prefer `args.get(1)` over `args[1]` to read the first argument?
options: `args[1]` panics if the argument is missing, while `.get(1)` returns an Option you can handle
quiz.explain: Indexing out of range panics. `.get(1)` gives Some/None so a missing argument becomes a case you handle, not a crash.

quiz.q: Where should a CLI print error and status messages?
quiz.explain: stdout is for the real result (so it can be piped/redirected cleanly); errors and status go to stderr via eprintln!.

quiz.q: What exit code should a CLI return when it fails?
options: It can't set an exit code
quiz.explain: 0 means success; non-zero means failure. Scripts rely on this, e.g. `myapp && echo ok` only runs if myapp exited 0.

flashcards.front: How do you read command-line arguments with just the standard library?
flashcards.back: `let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().collect();` — args[0] is the program name, real args start at args[1].

flashcards.front: stdout vs stderr — what goes where in a CLI?
flashcards.back: stdout (println!) = the real result/data. stderr (eprintln!) = status, warnings, errors. Keep them separate so piping works.

flashcards.front: How does a program report success or failure to the shell?
flashcards.back: Its exit code: 0 = success, non-zero = failure. Set it with std::process::exit(code) or return Result from main.

flashcards.front: When should you use the `clap` crate?
flashcards.back: For anything beyond one or two arguments. clap parses flags/options and generates --help, --version, and error messages for you.
